content: Urinary incontinence is a prevalent and often distressing condition that significantly impacts both social and psychological well-being. Many individuals rely on absorbent products to manage urine leakage and protect their clothing. Defining light urinary incontinence can be challenging, as the volume, flow, and frequency of urine loss can vary widely while still being categorized as light. This condition may range from occasional, minimal leaks (e.g., 1 to 2 grams of urine monthly) to frequent, larger leaks (e.g., 20 to 50 grams several times daily). A practical definition of light incontinence is urine loss that can be managed with a small absorbent pad, typically capable of holding 50 to 500 grams of fluid, as per ISO standards from 1996. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of various absorbent product designs for women experiencing light urinary incontinence. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Trials Register (as of April 2, 2009) and reviewed reference lists of relevant articles to identify eligible studies. The study selection criteria included randomized or quasi-randomized trials that investigated absorbent products designed for women with light urinary incontinence. The participants were women with this condition, and the interventions studied included different types of absorbent products, such as disposable insert pads, disposable menstrual pads, washable pants with an integrated pad, and washable insert pads. Two independent reviewers assessed the methodological quality of the studies and extracted data from the included trial. Only one study, involving 85 participants, met the inclusion criteria. This trial evaluated all the absorbent product designs under review and provided data on all relevant outcomes. The findings indicated that disposable insert pads were the most effective at preventing leakage, followed by disposable menstrual pads, washable pants with an integrated pad, and washable insert pads. In terms of user preference and overall acceptability, disposable insert pads were also rated the highest. However, there was no strong evidence to suggest that either disposable or washable products were superior for maintaining skin health. Disposable insert pads were identified as the most expensive option, and no single design emerged as the most cost-effective. It was noted that some women preferred alternative designs, which were generally less expensive than disposable inserts. The authors concluded that, despite data being available from only one eligible trial, the findings were robust enough to inform clinical practice. Disposable insert pads were found to be generally more effective than other designs. However, given their higher cost, offering a variety of product designs—or combinations of designs tailored to different circumstances—would likely be a more cost-effective approach.
